object-o.explain: を (said o) comes right after what the verb acts on, and the verb comes last: コーヒーを飲みます (coffee drink), 本を読みます (book read).
object-o.why: English shows what's drunk by putting it after the verb; Japanese marks it with を and keeps the verb for the end of the sentence.

examples.text: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。
私は牛乳とお水を飲みます。

contrasts.says: English says drink coffee; Japanese says coffee を drink, the verb last.
は marks who the sentence is about; を what the verb acts on.

mistakes.why: What's drunk takes を: が never goes on it with 飲みます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

question-ka.explain: か at the end of a sentence makes it a question; nothing else moves: 元気です (I'm well) → 元気ですか (are you well?). A question word sits where its answer would: どこですか (where is it?).
question-ka.why: English turns words around (Are you…? Do you…?); Japanese keeps the order and adds か, so the question is heard at the very end.

examples.text: コーヒーも飲みますか。

contrasts.says: English adds do or moves is to the front; Japanese adds か at the end.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

te-iru.explain: -ています says something is going on now: 読みます (I read) → 読んでいます (I'm reading); 飲みます → 飲んでいます.
te-iru.why: -ます alone says what you do, now or as a habit; -ています says it's going on right now, as English -ing does.

examples.text: 新聞を読んでいますか。
母は新聞を読んでいます。

contrasts.says: 読みます is what you do (I read); 読んでいます what's going on now (I'm reading).

mistakes.why: The form is 読んで, then います.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

topic-wa.explain: は (said wa) after a word makes it what the sentence is about: スマホは… (as for the phone…), 私は… (as for me…). What comes after says something about it.
topic-wa.why: English has no word for it: は sets the scene, and the rest of the sentence answers. It's written は but said wa.

examples.text: スマホはテーブルの上です。
examples.means: The phone is on the table.

contrasts.says: は says what you're talking about; が picks out who or what, often something new: 鍵があります.

mistakes.why: Who it's about takes は: を goes only on what's drunk.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

desu.explain: です after a noun or a place says what something is, or where: 車はここです (the car is here), 私の鍵です (it's my key). It's the same for I, you and it.
desu.why: English changes am, is and are; です never changes, and comes last.

contrasts.says: English has am, is and are; Japanese has です for all of them.

mistakes.why: です alone; だ and です are the same word, plain and polite.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

adjectives.explain: A word like いい (good) takes です to be polite, as every い adjective does: いいです (it's good). 準備はいいですか (is the getting-ready good?) asks if you're ready.
adjectives.why: English needs is before an adjective; in Japanese the い word already says it, and です only makes it polite.

contrasts.says: です after an い word makes it polite; after a noun it says what something is.

mistakes.why: An い adjective takes です straight after it, never だ.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

possessive-no.explain: の joins two nouns, the owner first: 私の鍵 (my key), 友達のスマホ (my friend's phone), 母の車 (Mom's car). After an owner alone it means the one of: 私のです (it's mine).
possessive-no.why: English has my, your and 's; Japanese puts の after the owner for all of them.

examples.text: 友達のかばんは車の中です。
examples.means: My friend's bag is in the car.

examples.text: このスマホは私のです。

contrasts.says: English says my, your, Mom's; Japanese says 私の, 母の: the owner and の.

mistakes.wrong: スマホはテーブルに上です。
mistakes.right: スマホはテーブルの上です。
mistakes.why: 上 (on) is a noun: the table joins it with の, as an owner does.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

aru-iru.explain: あります says a thing is there, います a person or animal: テーブルの上にお茶があります (there's tea on the table), 母は車の中にいます (Mom is in the car). Where takes に.
aru-iru.why: English uses is for both; Japanese asks whether it's alive: あります for a key or tea, います for Mom or a friend.

examples.text: テーブルの上にお茶があります。
examples.literal: Table's top on tea is there.

examples.text: かばんの中に鍵がありますか。
examples.means: Is there a key in the bag?
examples.literal: Bag's inside in key is there?

contrasts.says: English's is covers both; Japanese has あります for things, います for people and animals.

mistakes.wrong: テーブルの上にお茶がいます。
mistakes.right: テーブルの上にお茶があります。
mistakes.why: A thing is there with あります; います is for people and animals.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

particle-de.explain: で marks where you do something, に where you go: 家でお茶を飲みます (at home I drink tea); 家に帰ります (I go home).
particle-de.why: English uses at home and home for both; Japanese asks whether something is done there (で) or you go there (に).

examples.text: 母は家でコーヒーを飲みます。

contrasts.says: に is where you go, or where something is; で where something is done.

mistakes.why: Where you go takes に.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

masen.explain: -ません in place of -ます makes a verb not: 飲みます (drink) → 飲みません (don't drink), 帰ります → 帰りません. There's no do: the verb's ending says it.
masen.why: English adds do not; Japanese changes the ending of the verb itself.

examples.text: 私はコーヒーを飲みません。

contrasts.says: English adds don't or doesn't; Japanese changes -ます to -ません.

mistakes.wrong: コーヒーを飲むません。
mistakes.right: コーヒーを飲みません。
mistakes.why: The form is 飲みません.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

want-tai.explain: A verb's -ます part with たいです says what you want to do: 飲みます → 飲みたいです (I want to drink), 食べます → 食べたいです. What you want takes が or を.
want-tai.why: English says want to drink; Japanese adds たい to the verb itself, and です to stay polite.

contrasts.says: -たいです is what you want; -ましょう invites someone to do it with you.

mistakes.why: たい goes on the -ます part: 飲み.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

masu.explain: -ます is the same for I, you, he and she: 私は飲みます, 母は飲みます, 友達は飲みます. Who does it comes from は, or isn't said at all.
masu.why: English adds -s for he and she; a Japanese verb never changes for who does it.

contrasts.says: English says I drink, she drinks; Japanese says 飲みます for both.

mistakes.why: The form is 飲みます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

potential.explain: できます says can do: 何ができますか (what can I do?). A verb has a can form of its own: 手伝えます (can help), 読めます (can read). What you can takes が: 本が読めます.
potential.why: English adds can before the verb; Japanese changes the verb itself.

contrasts.says: English says can read; Japanese says 読めます, one word.

mistakes.why: The form is 読めます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

to-and.explain: と joins nouns: コーヒーとお茶 (coffee and tea). After a person it means with: 母と帰ります (I go home with Mom); 一緒に (together) often goes with it.
to-and.why: English has and and with; Japanese uses と for both, after the word it joins.

examples.text: コーヒーとお茶を飲みます。
私と一緒に帰りますか。
examples.means: Are you going home with me?

contrasts.says: English says with Mom; Japanese says 母と, と after the person.

mistakes.why: With someone takes と: を never goes with 帰ります.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

kosoado.explain: これ (this one) stands alone: これは私の鍵です. Before a noun it's この: この鍵 (this key). それ and その are that, near the one you're talking to.
kosoado.why: English's this works both ways; Japanese has これ on its own and この before a noun, and neither changes for the noun.

examples.text: このかばんは母のです。
それはだれのスマホですか。

contrasts.says: 私のです (it's mine) often follows: この鍵は私のです.

mistakes.why: Alone, it's これ; この needs a noun after it.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

subject-ga.explain: が marks what is there, or what you have, with あります: 仕事があります (work is there: I have work), 鍵があります (I have a key). With ありません, you don't.
subject-ga.why: English says I have; Japanese says the thing is there, marked with が.

contrasts.says: は is what you're talking about; が what's there, often new.

mistakes.why: What there is takes が: を never goes with あります.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

question-word.explain: だれ asks who, 何 what, どこ where, いつ when, and どうして why. Put the question word where the answer would go, and end with か. 予約は今日です becomes 予約はいつですか. When asking who does something, use だれが: だれが来ますか. 何 is なに before を here. The single words だれか and 何か mean someone and something, or anyone and anything in a question; their か does not make the whole sentence a question.
question-word.why: English often moves a question word to the front and adds do or changes the verb order. Japanese keeps the question word with the particle for its job. The verb or です still comes near the end, before the final か.

examples.text: スマホはどこにありますか。

contrasts.says: 予約はいつですか keeps when after the appointment; English asks When is the appointment?
A question word asks for a missing detail. Sentence-final か makes the sentence a question; the か inside だれか or 何か instead makes an indefinite word.
だれが来ますか asks who is coming. が marks the unknown person as the subject.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

hoshii.explain: Put the thing you want before が欲しいです: お水が欲しいです. 欲しい is an い adjective, so です makes it polite. 少し can say how much: お水が少し欲しいです. A question such as お水が欲しいですか asks the listener about their wants. Said plainly, 欲しいです is about your own wants, or asks the person you're talking to about theirs; what someone else wants is said another way, later.
hoshii.why: English uses the verb want for things and actions. Japanese uses 欲しい for a thing and a verb with たい for an action.

examples.text: お水が少し欲しいです。
もう少しお水が欲しいです。
examples.means: I want a little more water.

contrasts.says: お水が欲しいです wants water; お水を飲みたいです wants to drink water.
The Japanese adjective follows what is wanted. English puts want first.

mistakes.why: 欲しい takes です directly. Do not insert だ after an い adjective.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

adjective-negative.explain: For an い adjective, replace the final い with くない and keep です: 高いです becomes 高くないです, and 忙しいです becomes 忙しくないです; いい becomes よくないです. A な adjective keeps its word and takes じゃないです: 静かじゃないです. Both are everyday polite negatives. Having no money or time is different: お金がありません, 時間がありません. This rule does not make every word ending in い an い adjective.
adjective-negative.why: English adds not to is or am. Japanese changes the adjective’s ending, or uses the negative copula after a な adjective.

examples.text: このコーヒーは高くないです。
今日は忙しくないです。
この町は静かじゃないです。

contrasts.says: ありません says you do not have something. 忙しくないです says you are not busy.
高い changes to 高くない; 静か keeps its form before じゃないです.

mistakes.wrong: この町は静かじゃないだです。
mistakes.right: この町は静かじゃないです。
mistakes.why: The negative already ends in ない. Keep です directly after it, without だ.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

past-adjective.explain: An い adjective changes its final い to かった: 面白いです becomes 面白かったです, and いい becomes よかったです. The adjective itself says it was true in the past, while です remains the polite ending. A な adjective stays unchanged and uses でした: 静かでした. These lessons practise the affirmative past; other past forms come later.
past-adjective.why: English puts was or were before the adjective. Japanese uses two patterns, depending on the kind of adjective.

examples.text: 友達の話は面白かったです。
その話は面白かったです。
この部屋は静かでした。

contrasts.says: Verbs use -ました. An い adjective instead uses -かったです.
面白い changes its own ending; 静か keeps its form and uses でした.

mistakes.wrong: 友達の話は面白いでした。
mistakes.right: 友達の話は面白かったです。
mistakes.why: Do not put でした after the unchanged い adjective. Make the adjective past with かった.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

to-omou.explain: Put what you think before と, then finish with 思います. Use a verb’s dictionary form inside the thought: 来ます becomes 来る, 帰ります becomes 帰る, and 始まります becomes 始まる. 友達は五時に来ると思います means I think my friend will come at five. An い adjective needs no です before と: この映画は面白いと思います. This round uses only these affirmative nonpast thoughts. Noun and な-adjective thoughts, and the other plain forms, come later. Time and place keep their own particles; time before place is useful but not compulsory.
to-omou.why: English often starts with I think. Japanese saves 思います for the end, after the whole thought. A dictionary form inside it does not make the overall sentence casual.

examples.text: 映画は五時に始まると思います。
examples.means: I think the film starts at five.
examples.literal: Film five o'clock at starts think.

examples.text: 母はここに来ると思います。
examples.means: I think Mom will come here.

examples.text: 姉は五時に帰ると思います。
examples.means: I think my older sister will go home at five.
examples.literal: Older sister five o'clock at goes home think.

contrasts.says: 来ます is a polite verb ending on its own. Before と思います, this lesson uses 来る.
The と after a thought marks what you think. The と after a person can mean with.

mistakes.wrong: 母はここに来ると思うます。
mistakes.right: 母はここに来ると思います。
mistakes.why: 思う is the dictionary form. Its polite form is 思います, not the dictionary form with ます appended.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

kara-because.explain: Say the reason, add から, and then give the result: 電車が止まりましたから、遅れました. Keep the reason polite too: 時間がありますから or 忙しいですから. The ending before から still tells you whether that reason is present, past or negative. A comma can separate reason and result. This is different from から after a place or a time, which means from.
kara-because.why: English can put because and its reason after the result. These Japanese sentences put the reason first, with から at its end.

examples.text: 電車が止まりましたから、遅れました。
examples.means: I was late because the train stopped.

examples.text: 仕事がありますから、まだ会社にいます。
examples.means: I'm still at the office because I have work.
examples.literal: Work have because still office at am.

examples.text: お金がありませんから、家で食べます。
examples.means: I'll eat at home because I don't have any money.
examples.literal: Money don't have because home at eat.

contrasts.says: どうして asks why. A reason followed by から answers it.
から after a clause means because. After a time or a place it means from; that use is practised next.

mistakes.wrong: お金があるませんから、家で食べます。
mistakes.right: お金がありませんから、家で食べます。
mistakes.why: The reason keeps its correct negative form, ありません, before から.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

verb-particles.explain: Learn the whole pairing: 友達を待ちます means wait for a friend; 友達に会います means meet a friend; 電車に乗ります means get on or ride a train; 家を出ます means leave home. In 家を出ます, を marks the place you leave. It does not mean the house is an object you act on. These particles stay the same in the past. 会います also allows と when describing a mutual meeting, so と is not a wrong alternative to に. Where an action happens can still take で: 駅で友達に会いました.
verb-particles.why: English prepositions do not map one for one to Japanese particles. English says wait for a friend but meet a friend with no preposition, while Japanese uses を for the first and に for the second.

examples.text: ここで友達を待っています。
examples.means: I'm waiting for my friend here.
examples.literal: Here at friend am waiting for.

examples.text: 五時に友達に会います。
examples.means: I'll meet my friend at five.

contrasts.says: に can mark a destination, the person met, or a vehicle boarded. Learn its role with the verb.
を marks the person waited for and also the place left with 出ます.
友達と会います can describe a mutual meeting. It is valid, so it is not a distractor here.

mistakes.why: 待ちます takes を for the person you are waiting for.
会います does not take を for the person you meet.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

noun-modify.explain: Put the describing word before the noun. An い adjective needs no link: 面白い本 means interesting books, and 新しいペン means new pens. A な adjective takes な: 静かな部屋 means quiet rooms. きれい is a な adjective despite its final い, so use きれいな写真. Compare 部屋は静かです, a complete sentence, with 静かな部屋, a noun phrase. Do not keep です inside the noun phrase. The usual particles and counters then follow: 面白い本が二冊あります.
noun-modify.why: Both languages put these descriptions before nouns. Japanese also distinguishes the two adjective classes: only a な adjective takes な.

examples.text: 面白い本が二冊あります。
静かな部屋が二つあります。
きれいな写真が二枚あります。

contrasts.says: 部屋は静かです describes the room in a sentence. 静かな部屋 puts quiet inside the noun phrase.
母の本 links two nouns with の. 面白い本 uses an い adjective directly; 静かな部屋 uses a な adjective with な.

mistakes.wrong: 面白いです本が二冊あります。
mistakes.right: 面白い本が二冊あります。
mistakes.why: Do not carry the polite sentence ending です into a noun phrase. 面白い goes directly before 本.

mistakes.wrong: 静かです部屋が二つあります。
mistakes.right: 静かな部屋が二つあります。
mistakes.why: Before 部屋, 静か takes な, not the sentence ending です.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.

naide-kudasai.explain: To ask someone not to do something, put the verb in its ない form and add でください. 置く becomes 置かない: 本をそこに置かないでください means please do not put the book there. 開ける drops る before ない: このドアを開けないでください means please do not open this door. These examples introduce the ない form within polite requests; using it as a casual sentence ending comes later. Keep the same particles for the thing and place. ません is the polite negative ending, but it cannot go directly before ください.
naide-kudasai.why: English adds do not after please. Japanese changes the verb to its negative form and uses でください after it.

examples.text: 本をそこに置かないでください。
examples.means: Please don't put the book there.

examples.text: このドアを開けないでください。
まだドアを開けないでください。
examples.means: Please don't open the door yet.

contrasts.says: 置いてください asks someone to put something down. 置かないでください asks them not to.
置きません says I will not put it there. 置かないでください asks someone else not to put it there.

mistakes.wrong: 本をそこに置きませんください。
mistakes.right: 本をそこに置かないでください。
mistakes.why: A negative request uses 置かないで before ください, not the polite negative 置きません.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.

purpose.explain: Say why someone goes, comes or returns with a verb stem plus に: 飲みます loses ます to become 飲み, so お茶を飲みに行きます means go to drink tea. 会います gives 会い: 兄に会いに行きます means go to meet my older brother. The first に marks the person met; the second marks the purpose. The last verb carries politeness, and can be 行きます, 来ます, 帰ります or an invitation such as 行きましょう. An activity noun also works: 散歩に行きます means go for a walk. This is a purpose construction with movement; it is not a general translation of every English to plus verb.
purpose.why: English says go to drink or come to meet. Japanese puts the intended activity first, then に and the motion verb.

examples.text: お茶を飲みに行きます。
examples.means: I'm going to have some tea.
I'm going to see my older brother.
I'm going home to see Mom.

examples.text: この公園は安全です。散歩に行きましょう。
examples.means: This park is safe. Let's go for a walk.
examples.literal: This park safe is. A walk for let's go.

contrasts.says: 学校に行きます gives a destination. 飲みに行きます gives the purpose of going.
兄に会いに行きます has two に particles: the person met after 兄, and the purpose after 会い.

mistakes.wrong: お茶を飲むに行きます。
mistakes.right: お茶を飲みに行きます。
mistakes.why: Purpose uses the ます stem 飲み, not the dictionary form 飲む.
Use the stem 会い before the purpose に, not the dictionary form 会う.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.
